keyPoints: Chapter 2
Designing Robust C++ Classes
Modern C++ lecture with code, output, and presenter script
slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 2: Designing Robust C++ Classes. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

question.prompt: What is the central teaching rule for Modern C++?
question.answer: Do not praise an abstraction until you can explain the rule it encodes and the evidence that proves it behaves correctly.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Designing Robust C++ Classes changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 2.1 Establishing Strong Class Invariants
keyPoints: An invariant describes all states that a successfully constructed object may expose during ordinary use.
For Percentage, the value is between zero and one hundred inclusive.
Validation belongs at every state-changing entry point, not only the constructor.
A class can prevent invalid states more effectively when the representation is private and the public interface.

slides.title: 2.1.2 Restricting Mutation Through Interfaces
keyPoints: The setter validates the candidate before assigning it.
Rejection therefore leaves the old percentage unchanged.
This is a local strong-guarantee pattern: perform the fallible check first, then commit a simple nonthrowing.
Do not expose a mutable reference to the private value, because that would bypass validation.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat 2.1.2 Restricting Mutation Through Interfaces as a design decision with costs and evidence. The setter validates the candidate before assigning it. Rejection therefore leaves the old percentage unchanged. This is a local strong-guarantee pattern: perform the fallible check first, then commit a simple nonthrowing scalar assignment. Do not expose a mutable reference to the private value, because that would bypass validation. Likewise, a bulk-update operation involving several fields must validate their relationship as a whole rather than calling independent setters that temporarily create inconsistent combinations. The invariant belongs to the object, not to a checklist of field names. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat 2.2.1 Designing Const Member Functions as a design decision with costs and evidence. int value() const noexcept is a small read-only query that returns an independent scalar. A const object can use it without giving the caller a path to mutate the representation. The noexcept specification is appropriate because this simple query performs no throwing operation. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat 2.2.2 Passing Data Without Unnecessary Mutation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The reading collection’s at query returns an integer value from checked access, while replace is a separate mutating operation. Calling a mutator on a const collection is rejected by the type system. This makes the code’s intent clearer than a single accessor that returns a mutable reference in every context. Passing read-only data by const reference can avoid copying, but returning a small scalar by value is often simpler than exposing a long-lived borrow. Decide where the lifetime boundary should be. A fast-looking reference return is a poor interface when callers can retain it after the owner changes or disappears. slides.title: 2.3.1 Delegating Resource Management to Library Types
keyPoints: Readings owns a vector of integers.
The vector already knows how to release storage, copy elements, and transfer ownership through moves.
The enclosing class can therefore focus on its public behavior instead of manually allocating and freeing an array.
The constructor accepts a vector by value and moves that local value into the member.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat 2.3.1 Delegating Resource Management to Library Types as a design decision with costs and evidence. Readings owns a vector of integers. The vector already knows how to release storage, copy elements, and transfer ownership through moves. The enclosing class can therefore focus on its public behavior instead of manually allocating and freeing an array. The constructor accepts a vector by value and moves that local value into the member. This gives a straightforward ownership boundary: callers can provide a temporary or an existing collection, and the class owns its resulting member. The exact copy cost depends on the argument and is a deliberate consequence of the interface, not hidden raw-pointer borrowing. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat Establish the accepted-state boundary as a design decision with costs and evidence. Start the percentage at forty and attempt to replace it with 101. The crucial assertion is the one after rejection: the object must still report forty. Testing only that an exception occurred would miss a setter that assigned 101 before throwing. The endpoint checks then clarify that the range is inclusive. Test names should state those distinctions rather than collecting them under an opaque “works” label. For readings, perform a copy and then change one element in the copy. The vector’s value semantics should keep the original element unchanged. This is a separate requirement from percentage validity, and the example intentionally checks both. Together they demonstrate that class correctness has several dimensions: local domain invariants, ownership, and copy behavior. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Failure clinic — Validation after mutation
keyPoints: The tempting setter writes its candidate into the field and then calls a validation function.
Its happy path looks identical to the correct setter.
Its failure path leaves an invalid object behind.
A later unrelated query may expose the defect, making the original cause difficult to locate.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat Failure clinic — Validation after mutation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The tempting setter writes its candidate into the field and then calls a validation function. Its happy path looks identical to the correct setter. Its failure path leaves an invalid object behind. A later unrelated query may expose the defect, making the original cause difficult to locate. Reverse the order and make the transition visible: compute an accepted candidate, then commit it. For a single integer, the final assignment is simple. For a collection, a candidate object and a suitable nonthrowing swap can provide a stronger boundary. Do not generalize the integer example into “all assignment is nonthrowing”; the member operations of the actual type determine that property. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Guided lab — Replace a validated interval atomically
keyPoints: Build an interval value with two integer endpoints.
Successful construction and replacement require the first endpoint to be no greater than the last.
Expose read-only endpoint queries and one replacement operation taking both candidates.
Avoid separate unrestricted reference accessors.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 2, treat Guided lab — Replace a validated interval atomically as a design decision with costs and evidence. Build an interval value with two integer endpoints. Successful construction and replacement require the first endpoint to be no greater than the last. Expose read-only endpoint queries and one replacement operation taking both candidates. Avoid separate unrestricted reference accessors. Use accepted intervals entirely below zero, crossing zero, and reduced to a single point. Attempt an inverted interval after a successful construction and compare both endpoints before and after rejection. Then replace the interval with a disjoint valid interval and verify that no caller needs to create an invalid intermediate state.
